title: Calef's More Wonders of the Invisible World: Devastating Critique of Salem
description: Robert Calef, a Boston merchant, published More Wonders of the Invisible World in 1700 (printed in London), a systematic critique of the Salem prosecutions and of Cotton Mather's defense of them in Wonders of the Invisible World (1693). Calef documented procedural irregularities, challenged the reliability of spectral evidence, and attacked Mather's role in encouraging the prosecutions. The book was controversial enough that Increase Mather reportedly had copies burned in Harvard Yard. Calef's text, together with the formal apologies of some Salem participants and Samuel Sewall's public confession of error (1697), represents the early colonial American process of disowning the trials — a process with no real parallel in European witch-trial history.
historiographical_note: The Mather-Calef controversy has been extensively analyzed as a conflict between different models of evidence and authority in colonial New England. Cotton Mather's reputation suffered severely from Calef's attack, and the historiography of Salem has been shaped by this contemporary controversy — historians have often positioned themselves relative to the Calef/Mather debate.
source_method: Calef, More Wonders of the Invisible World (1700); secondary scholarship on Salem and its aftermath
